newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail, building data.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Australian retail, building data.

text.p: Australian retail trade rose 2.9 percent in May, following on from a 1.7 percent fall in April, offical figures showed on Wednesday.
Forecasts for retail trade had centred on a 2.0 percent rise, and ranged from a 0.2 percent fall to a 3.0 percent rise.
Separate data showed building approvals rose 2.2 percent in May.
Forecasts had centred on a 2.0 percent rise and ranged from a 3.0 percent fall to a rise to 10.0 percent.
A selection of economists' reactions to the data follows.
CRAIG JAMES, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COLONIAL STATE BANK

"A little bit above market expectations. It's important not to get too carried away with the figures, though, as both indicators are volatile on a month-to-month basis. Trend growth of retail trade is now about 0.3 percent a month, annual growth is now about 2.6 percent, so you can see retail trade growth remains very modest. Yes, we have got a rise in building approvals but to date the recovery in building approvals is around half the pace of recovery in 1991. I don't think it changes the view of policy one way or the other. Activity still remains fairly modest and we do expect a further easing in interest rates."
STEPHEN ROBERTS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, UBS AUSTRALIA:

"For retail sales, even with the 2.9 percent monthly rise it is more of a rebound from the two very soft months we had running before, so it doesn't necessarily shift the outlook all that much. For home building approvals, the 6.3 percent increase in private sector houses looks reasonably firm but it depends on whether the Olympic Village is in there yet. If it is, then it is not all that strong a number. I don't think either of the figures in themselves are strong enough to change conditions that much."
MICHAEL BLYTHE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, COMMONWEALTH BANK OF AUSTRALIA:

"Unfortunately I don't think it (retail) really gives us the definitive answer we have been looking for. A bounce back was always on the cards after April's figure. We will have to wait for next week's numbers to get a better idea of the trend. Spending is rising reasonably, it's not roaring, it's not falling in a hole. On the rate front, it slightly reduces the chance of another rate cut."
KAREN PRINGLE, SENIOR TREASURY ECONOMIST, ANZ BANK:

"They're right at the top end (of expectations) so I suppose if anything they do change the picture a little bit the view that we had of retail spending. But it doesn't restore it to anywhere near potential growth, and we've still the risks of fiscal policy detracting from growth, significant excess capacity in the economy and a pretty good inflation picture, so the Reserve Bank could still cut rates again in that enviroment despite the fact that these numbers are on the high side."
JOHN EDWARDS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, HSBC MARKETS:

"I think (Reserve Bank of Australia governor) Ian Macfarlane will likely ignore the building approvals as being too much influenced by the Olympic village but he won't ignore the retail sales which is a very strong result. It's only one argument, and it is not conclusive, but it is an argument against a rate cut."
JOHN KYRIAKOPOULOS, SENIOR ECONOMIST, J.P MORGAN:

"On the retail side, I suppose the number was stronger than market expectations, that is stating the obvious. But for us it is more a rebound to earlier weakness than a sign of strength. In the two prior months, retail spending had fallen by two percent in total and we are now 0.9 ahead over three months so retail spending is only travelling along at a very moderate pace and is certainly not strong enough at this stage to preclude another rate reduction by the RBA (Reserve Bank of Australia). The building approvals data is very difficult to assess, because particularly in the private sector component just about all the increase in approvals, certainly house approvals, was related to the (Sydney 2000) Olympic project. So once you take those out of the equation the number was pretty flat."
STEPHEN KOUKOULAS, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CITIBANK AUSTRALIA:

"It's a mixed bag from our reading of it. The retail sales numbes are a little bit stronger than we thought but nonetheless it is really only recovering the last two monthly falls and if you look at the dollar value of retail trade in the month it is only a little bit above where we were at the beginning of the year. So I wouldn't say the retail sector is booming yet, it is encouraging to see a bit of growth coming through but I think the best you could say is the worst is behind us. The pre-conditions are there for an upswing but how strong that upswing is is the $64 question at the moment. Building is a mixed bag, it seems some of the Olympic Games has got its way into approvals. My quick look through it suggests that without the Olympic Games we would have had a negative, which is a surprise given the wonderful affordability in the housing sector at the moment."
